The Tribunal's south-western quarter: Serbia, Bosnia and Croatia, with the Istrian peninsula and the Adriatic shore beyond the Dinaric Alps. The Slavs came south over the Danube in the sixth and seventh centuries, from a homeland no chronicle can place; by 1220 they are too many tribes to list, and only the Serbs, the Bosniaks (Bošnjanin) and the Croats have become powers. Smaller groups live among their neighbours: the Krashovani by the Timok, the Šokci on the Sava, the Gorani on the edge of Epiros, the Montenegrins of Zeta, and the Székely in the eastern Carpathians.

A Slav household is a zadruga, an extended family under its patriarch, living in a knot of half-sunken log huts; herders and farmers, a clan can load its goods and drive its beasts away overnight when danger comes. Most villages lie open by rivers and lakes, though a few north of the Danube shelter the chieftain's kin behind an earth bank and palisade ringed with hidden wolf-pits. Every Slav offers a stranger a meal and a seat at his table, and many still burn their dead on a pyre with their goods, which the clergy condemn and the townsfolk are giving up. Few are professional soldiers; a spear and a small wooden shield are the usual arms, and the Serbs fight in the Byzantine manner they have absorbed.

The Old Ways. Every Slav tribe is Christian now, but many simply gave their old high god, Perun the Thunderer, the name God and kept the rest; priests call this double faith, dvoeverie, and find it strongest north of the Danube. Perun rules the sky and guards the World Tree, forever hunting Veles, a dragon of the underworld, trickery and magic, who steals his cattle, is slain, sinks below and returns; some still hear their fight in every thunderstorm. Pilgrims seek the old holy places, fenced clearings in deep woods or on lonely heights with many-headed idols of Perun, watched over by werewolves. Many such sites carry Magic auras, not Faerie, so Hermetic theorists suspect Perun and Veles were titans of the Magic realm and that lost magical traditions wait to be found there; the Order holds several, Rügen, the Bjornaer domus magna, among them.

Perun's golden apples, thrown skyward to burst into a storm of lightning (a Serbian tale has one killing six hundred), are his mightiest weapon. Several Tremere would dearly like one for the House's arsenal; none has ever been found.

Vis in the region (each in its place): Perun's stones and arrows in the Pirin Mountains (Auram), and, held by the Histrian oppida, Old Histria's mercury pool (Terram), the Istrian truffles (Herbam), the Strange Vis of the roof tar (Creo), Cres's blood well (Corpus) and storm beach (Rego); also the amphorae of Pula's temple, and the blood in a destroyed strigon's grave.

neighbours.name: The Sacred Glens of Perun
neighbours.summary: The holy places of the old Slav faith, spread through the forests and mountains of the Slav lands: clearings closed by a wooden fence, some with a carved idol of Perun in wood or stone showing several heads, and guarded, the old writings say, by werewolves. Pagan pilgrims still come. Where magi have looked, the auras are often Magic (of no stated strength), which is why some think Perun and Veles were titans, and a seeker might find a lost tradition among those who keep only the old religion.

neighbours.name: The Pirin Mountains
neighbours.summary:
A mountain range where lightning has fused the soil into Perun's stones, fulgurites: hollow tubes of natural glass two or three inches across and up to several feet long, most holding a pawn or two of Auram vis, found by travellers across the range.

Longer ones, Perun's arrows, turn up only in Magic auras. Their vis is spell-like: hurled like a javelin, one becomes a bolt of lightning before it strikes (a CrAu 25 effect, +30 damage on a hit, Initiative -1 and Attack +1 as a thrown weapon). Not yet in the item catalog.

neighbours.name: Serbia
neighbours.summary:
The western edge of the Tribunal, where the Balkans meet eastern Mythic Europe: first settled between the Sava and Danube to the north, the Morava to the east and the Adriatic to the south-west. Mountains, broken hills and plains, cut by many rivers, with the foothills of the Balkan range, the Carpathians and the Alps all reaching in, and the Dinaric Alps walling the coast off from the interior; the coast is Mediterranean, the inland weather much like Hungary's. Most people live in the fertile river valleys along the trade routes.

Serb legend says a great anchorite led them south at the bidding of Emperor Heraclius, to serve as Roman mercenaries, only for the emperor to bar them from the richest land. Each clan (župa) belongs to a district (župaija) under a chieftain, the župan; the župan of Raška, on the Bulgarian border, rose to be grand župan, and his line has ruled since, keeping the realm whole by playing Bulgaria and Byzantium off against each other.

The line between the pope's flock and the patriarch's runs through Serbia: Croatia is Roman, Bosnia goes its own way, and most Serbian dioceses took the Western rite when the papal legate crowned Stefan, though Kotor Bay and Ston keep the Greek one. Serbs are unusually easy about such differences; the strain lies between priests who cannot say the Latin rite and the superiors who demand it, which Rome tolerates for now.

neighbours.name: Studenica
neighbours.summary:
The white marble monastery at the head of the Raška, some fifteen miles north of Ras: the royal foundation that is the heart of the Serbian Church and Archbishop Sava's seat, and the holiest place in Serbia, with a Divine aura of 8. Inside its walls stand two churches, the Virgin's and the King's, both raised by Stefan Nemanja, blending Italian and Byzantine building into something admired on both sides.

The newly painted frescoes of the four portals hold a mythic artist's small wonders (Art & Academe): the sky behind the Crucifixion is blue by day, gold at sunset and black by night. Inside, one fresco shows Nemanja and the Virgin presenting a little model of the church to Christ.

St Stefan Nemanja's relics were brought here from Mount Athos in 1206, and his tomb has wept holy oil ever since, earning him the name Myrrh-flowing: enough each day to fill a small vial, and all day on his feast, 13 February. Anointing someone with a vial works one of a saint's miracles costing 1 Divine Might (Realms of Power: The Divine). The saint, of Divine Might 50, takes a close interest in his family and his church.

neighbours.name: Mount Hum
neighbours.summary:
A mountain of gentle slopes in the north of Zachlumia, on the Adriatic shore, the favourite hunting ground of King Stefan's eldest sons, Radoslav (28) and Vladislav (26), children of the queen he drove out for adultery in 1200, Eudocia Angelina. Since Serbian tales so often star a prince, the local faeries see the pair as perfect sources of vitality and keep dragging them into faerie adventures, which the princes, keener on game than on faeries, have no idea how to escape.

A few of the Tribunal's magi know of this and quietly help the princes out, anonymously where they can, careful neither to harm the faeries much nor to meddle visibly in mundane affairs. The book gives no aura.

neighbours.name: Bosnia
neighbours.summary:
A landlocked banate on the Dinaric Alps, with Hungary to the north, Croatia westward and Serbia on its southern and eastern sides, its northern edge reaching down into the Pannonian basin as far as the Sava and the Danube. Mostly hills and mountains; seven great rivers run off to the Adriatic, the Neretva, which divides Bosnia from Serbia and lower down Serbia from Croatia, the greatest of them. Settlements follow the rivers: Vrhbosna, the ban's seat and the heart of its church, Banja Luka in the north-west and Zenica on the Bosna.

Its own church, the Bosnian Church of the Patarians, is Bogomil in all but name, and the King of Hungary demands it be purged; following history, a Hungarian invasion is coming (see the Bosnian crusade among the threats).

neighbours.name: The Mansio of Vrhbosna
neighbours.summary: One of House Mercere's oldest mansiones, a half-public trading post in Vrhbosna with a name for trouble: quarrels every day and frequent brawls. Last year two local merchants came to blows there and one died; no visiting magus or servant was involved.
neighbours.secrets: Some suspect an Infernal aura has grown in the mansio; none has yet been detected.

neighbours.name: Croatia
neighbours.summary:
The border of west and east: the Italian communes on one side, Serbs, Bosniaks and Magyars on the other. The Alpine foothills reach its west, the green Pannonian valleys lie to the north, the wooded Dinaric Alps close the east, and the rocky Adriatic shore runs along the south, most of it paying tribute to Venice.

The Croats came south with the other Slavs and settled as two duchies, Pannonia in the north and Littoral Croatia on the coast; Frankish rule in the eighth century taught them feudal ways early, and their own kings ruled from the tenth century until the Trpimirović line ended in a feud between brothers in 1091. The northern nobles then offered the crown to Ladislaus I of Hungary, and Croatia has been a Hungarian vassal ever since.

neighbours.name: The Night Streets of Zadar
neighbours.summary:
Years of murder on Zadar's docks and back alleys have raised Infernal auras in the city, and over the worst killings Infernal regiones have formed. Greed, bloodshed and resentment draw demons, and some magi fear the city will become a centre of their work unless the tension eases; would-be demon hunters among the young magi boast of stalking its empty streets after dark. The book gives no aura strengths.

The zenodochium the Tremere hid here after 1203, and lost, is the hidden fortresses' (see the zenodochia).

neighbours.name: Diocletian's Palace
neighbours.summary:
The vast limestone palace the emperor Diocletian built near Salona, where he was born, and retired to; later governments used it as offices, and refugees and the persecuted long sought shelter in it. Legend says Cyril and Methodius devised the Glagolitic letters in one of its halls to put the Gospels into Old Slavonic. In 1220 it is a ruin, but not an empty one: Salona's monks dig for martyrs' relics, and treasure hunters roam the unexplored rooms after the emperor's gold.

Tremere magi now and then come looking for the dragon said to lie inside, coiled round a hoard of Roman gold. The current guess is that it lives in a regio; no one knows whether it is a Magic beast or an Infernal one, so the Magic 3 here is the pack's choice, not the book's.

neighbours.name: Istria
neighbours.summary:
The large peninsula at the head of the Adriatic, with its islands, claimed by the Histrian oppida; it takes its name, through the Romans, from the tribe that held it when Rome came. The coasts are Mediterranean; to the north-west the land climbs through wooded hills of pine and oak into low mountains. Many faeries live here, some very powerful.

Istria's vampire is the strigon, which roams the streets after midnight knocking on doors to foretell a death, lies with widows and drinks children's blood. It is hard to destroy unless caught at rest in a grave that is itself hard to find; dug up and staked through the belly, it leaves its grave full of blood rich in vis, more the older it was. Redcaps who travel by night loathe strigons, which attack them or get them chased by mobs as suspects, and the Mercere often ask Pahniro to deal with one (see the Bestiary).

A race of wise, friendly dragons, zmajevi, lives in Istria too, and the Histrian magi deal with them often (see the Bestiary and the Dragon War).

neighbours.name: The Fortress of Old Histria
neighbours.summary:
A hill fort older than Rome on a mountain north-east of Pazin, its ditches and walls rebuilt again and again over the centuries into deep layers of defence against any mundane assault, and guarded by potent enchanted items: the oppidum of Old Histria. Its Magic aura is 7.

In its grounds lies a pool of magical mercury, a rich source of Terram vis. A child dipped in it gains the Visions Flaw, and often worse Flaws besides, so it is seldom done.

The site is bleak in winter, cold and wet, which drives many of its magi to Cres for the season.

neighbours.name: The Truffle Woods of Northern Istria
neighbours.summary: Pine and oak forests rich in truffles, which are Herbam vis as well as a delicacy; magi think they grow best where lightning has struck, and pay their weight in gold for them. They are gathered by night by odd, silent men in dark cloaks with clever dogs. Faeries crave truffles and pester anyone who finds them, unless the finder knows the right propitiations.

neighbours.name: The Mirna Valley
neighbours.summary: A river valley of Istria where giants lived in ancient times; they are rare on the peninsula now. (The source text breaks off here.)

neighbours.name: The Arena of Pula
neighbours.summary:
Pula's amphitheatre, which magi credit to Rome and the town's faeries to themselves: building faeries raised it in a single night and fled at a muddled cock's crow before the roof was on, leaving a trail of huge stones dropped on the way from their far-off quarry. It stands open to the sky with a Faerie aura of 6, rising to 8 on certain nights; players who perform there then may cross into another world, or win favours from the unseen watchers beyond the back rows.

Those who have slipped into its regio tell of a faerie town beneath, Diviægrad, whose folk answer a visitor's needs or mock mortal life; magi hope the strange symbolism behind their games preserves something of Pula's founders, the Colchian war band sent after the Golden Fleece, ruled by a family of sorcerers, one of whom could turn back age.

The building faeries (Diviæe, see the Bestiary) are small and weak alone but achieve wonders together; given stone and a good reason they can raise a hall overnight, and what they build has a useful aura. Attempts to tame and spread them had mixed results and have stopped. The surest, and most perilous, way to their help is to go down into their town and find their rulers, or to bargain with the watchers at a play on an auspicious night. Swarms of small building faeries (Brownies of Realms of Power: Faerie) raised the Arena of Pula in a single night, left unfinished when a confused cock crowed early; what they build carries an aura, and their leaders, or the hidden watchers in the arena's back row on auspicious nights, can be bargained with.

neighbours.name: The Temple of Augustus, Pula
neighbours.summary:
A temple to the goddess Roma in the middle of Pula, with a Magic aura of 5; Seekers are sure it was once a place of power of the Cult of Mercury, but the town around it makes quiet study hard. Old amphorae keep working up out of the ground nearby, to be knocked by gardeners and passers-by; they hold vis but are awkward to gather.

King Solomon of Hungary, a folk hero rumoured to have founded the Scholomance, is buried in Pula.

neighbours.name: Mount Klek
neighbours.summary:
A mountain east of the Histrian lands, where witches and corrupted elves dance to demonic music. Its summit has a strong Infernal aura (no number is given) and perhaps a gate into Hell; witches are common all round it.

Local lore: a dust devil spinning up at a crossroads by night is two witches fighting, tearing at each other's hair, and a traveller must not walk through it; whoever has, comes back next morning and lays a stone on the spot to give away any curse he took.

neighbours.name: Cres
neighbours.summary:
An island ruled by Venice, one of a chain that folklore says the enchantress Medea made from the torn body of her brother Aspytrus, sent after the Golden Fleece and her lover; its faeries swear the tale is true, and the faint Magic aura of 1 over most of the island seems to bear it out.

Rego vis is cast up on one beach after storms, among ships' flotsam, building up through the year rather than coming once; a well of blood gives a large Corpus source. Both are Shrouded Bay's.

neighbours.name: The Villa of Shrouded Bay
neighbours.summary: The Histrian magi's large villa on Cres, hidden by The Shrouded Glen, in a Magic aura of 6: the oppidum of Shrouded Bay, pleasanter than Old Histria and the favourite winter home of its magi, with the Tremere and Mercere fleets' support works in the bay.

neighbours.name: The Grave of Aspytrus
neighbours.summary:
The palatial tomb where Medea laid her brother after raising Cres on his body as the focus of her spell. His servants, too frightened of her father to go home to Colchis, founded a city near Pula; when Jason cast her off she lived among them a while, and rid them of a plague of magical serpents by shutting the snakes into the tomb.

The magi of Cres leave it alone: Medea's curses may still guard it, and the serpents inside may be orms, wingless and legless dragons, or votaress snakes (zmije zatocnice), clever, vicious faerie snakes sworn not to sleep through winter until they have killed a man (see the Bestiary). Loosing a swarm of them just to see what they guard seems excessive.
neighbours.secrets: Some Seekers think Medea made her brother an airy spirit fit to be patron of a mystery cult, the serpents perhaps part of its Ordeals. A few magi desperate for her secret of regeneration have died to strong wards trying to break in; whether Medea, the Histrians or a cult already serving Aspytrus set them is unknown.

neighbours.name: Kingdom of Serbia
neighbours.summary:
The strongest of the Slav realms, ruled by the Nemanja line, the grand župans of Raška. Stefan Nemanja, of modest birth, rose as a Byzantine vassal, fought Hungary for the emperor in 1164, then rebelled and beat a Byzantine army at Pantino; his 1171 league with Venice, Hungary and German princes against Byzantium fell apart in Serbian feuds, Venetian mutiny and plague, and Manuel Komnenos besieged Ras and took him to Constantinople in chains. Oddly, the two became friends, and Nemanja came home the emperor's strategos and the Serbs' only lawful ruler. He gave up the throne in 1195, died in 1199 and was made a saint in 1200, a staunch Orthodox builder of churches and hammer of the Bogomils.

He passed over his eldest, Vukan, for his second son Stefan, and Vukan's anger brought civil war in 1204, the year the Latins took Constantinople. Stefan won, but too weakened to grab any lost Byzantine land, he bound the Serbian principalities into one kingdom instead, and in 1217 a papal legate crowned him king and autocrat of all the Serbian and coastal lands, the equal of Hungary's and Bulgaria's kings. His first wife, Eudocia Angelina, the emperor Alexios's daughter and mother of five of his children, he drove out for adultery in 1200; his second is Ana Dandolo, the doge Enrico Dandolo's daughter. With Stefan on the throne and his brother Sava over the Church, the Nemanjas hold the realm together, though Serbia's wealth and arms are a shadow of Hungary's or Bulgaria's, and Hungarian backing for Bosnia and Croatia, and Serbian feuding, keep Stefan from taking them.

Crowned by both Churches' representatives, Stefan has a Magic Resistance of 10 and, as a king of Slav blood, the Divine Shapeshifter Virtue: he can become a wolf, a lion, or even a dragon, as he pleases.

Two custos envoys of Kezdö Válasz attend his court with the Tribunal's leave, reporting to Essedarius and Leona: never advisers, never threats, they simply keep the Order in the king's mind and let slip, over dinner, the news of Hungary, Bulgaria, Latins and Greeks, giants, vampires and stirring dragons. Their careful reports go to Kezdö Válasz and on to Coeris, often carried by young Tremere. A seed: the pair are framed for some crime and await execution in Stefan's dungeon, their reports seized; the players must find who framed them and why.

neighbours.name: Banate of Bosnia
neighbours.summary:
A frontier province ruled by a ban, a rank like a duke's or a Serbian grand župan's; the present ban, whom the book does not name, is the King of Hungary's vassal, and the king holds the real power. Bosnia is weaker than Serbia, and Hungary keeps Stefan from swallowing it.

The king's letters order Bosnia's church to purge its Patarians; it answers that there are no heretics in Bosnia. The pope (Honorius III; the book says Honorius II) has sent a legate urging Andrew II to crusade, knights are mustering and preachers denounce the heretics, and House Tremere, barred from meddling yet sure a crusade could remake the Tribunal, cannot decide what to do (see the Bosnian crusade among the threats). In history nothing comes of it until 1237.

neighbours.name: Banate of Croatia
neighbours.summary: Croatia under the Árpád kings of Hungary since 1091: the Croats run their own affairs within the limits of vassalage, through a ban and twelve deputies who govern and lead the army. They insist the King of Hungary has no say unless he stands on Croatian soil and that no Hungarian may settle there, claims that are more story than truth. To Hungary it is a buffer in the west against the grasping Italian provinces and the Empire. Most of its coast pays tribute to Venice, and the nobles of Knin do nothing about it.
neighbours.ruler: The Ban of Croatia and his twelve deputies

neighbours.name: Republic of Venice
neighbours.summary: The merchant republic across the Adriatic, outside the Tribunal, which holds much of its coast: Zadar since 1202 (by a sham treaty since 1205), Dubrovnik since 1205, and the island of Cres, where Shrouded Bay stands. Most of the Croatian shore pays it tribute, and Dubrovnik is a base for its war galleys. The Histrian oppida keep a chapter house in the city.

neighbours.name: Studenica Monastery
neighbours.summary:
The royal monastery at the head of the Raška, centre of the Serbian Church and seat of its archbishop, holding St Stefan Nemanja's oil-weeping tomb (see the place).

Sava, born Rastko, Nemanja's youngest son, matters to the Serbs perhaps more than his royal brother. He fled his family's quarrels to the monks of Mount Athos, came back to Studenica in 1208 to build up the Serbian Church, and in 1219 won from the Greek patriarch its independence, the right to choose its own bishops, and was himself consecrated its archbishop. He wrote the Nomocanon, the great book of church law every Slavic church uses. Blessed by God, he has the Holy Method Invocation, with Wonders, Blessing and Adjuration among his Holy Powers (see Realms of Power: The Divine).

neighbours.name: The Cathedral School of Mostre
neighbours.summary: The cathedral school of the Bosnian Church at Mostre, with Veszprém's the nearest thing the region has to a university: it teaches theology, cosmology, ethics and medicine.

neighbours.name: Ras
neighbours.summary: Serbia's capital, in the middle of Raška, the Nemanja family's own district. Serbian troops took it from Byzantium in the Hungarian-Byzantine war of 1127 to 1129; burnt and rebuilt, it keeps little of the old town. New stone walls crown a gorge above the crossing of the main roads east-west and north-south. Smaller than Hungary's or Bulgaria's capitals, Ras with Novi Pazar is still the kingdom's political, cultural and religious centre.

neighbours.name: Novi Pazar
neighbours.summary: The 'new bazaar', a young trading town at the crossroads below Ras, which merchants prefer to the fortress: the royal market, though Ras's walls far above do not shelter it. The king's law holds, but trade is freer than elsewhere, so goods and people of every sort mix there. A backwater with few foreigners, it is where news is swapped and tales told, and a favourite spot for magi to meet agents and companions discreetly.

neighbours.name: Dubrovnik
neighbours.summary: Ragusa to the Italians: a lovely Adriatic port living on sea trade, walled in stone from its Byzantine days with double walls, round and square towers and attached forts, a wonder of the age. It once rivalled Venice, Genoa and Amalfi, and its riches undid it: Venice took it in 1205, and it now pays tribute and harbours Venetian galleys. Natives and occupiers dislike each other, down to the city's very name; some look to the Nemanjas for help, others to Byzantium. No blood has been shed yet, unlike Zadar, but House Tremere watches it closely.

neighbours.name: Vrhbosna
neighbours.summary: Bosnia's chief town, the forerunner of Sarajevo: seat of the ruling family and centre of the Bosnian Church, with one of House Mercere's oldest mansiones (see the place).

neighbours.name: Banja Luka
neighbours.summary: The 'duke's meadow', one of Bosnia's largest settlements, in the north-west.

neighbours.name: Zenica
neighbours.summary: One of Bosnia's largest settlements, on the River Bosna.

neighbours.name: Knin
neighbours.summary: The old royal capital of Croatia, at the source of the Krka on the site of the Roman camp of Burnum, under a mighty fortress. It stands for Croatian unity on a coast Venice dominates and is counted the steadying hand of the Croatian shore, yet it shows Croatia's weakness too: the coast pays Venice tribute and Knin's nobles sit still.

neighbours.name: Zadar
neighbours.summary: Zara to the Italians, the richest port of the Croatian coast and the King of Hungary's by right. Crusaders sacked it in 1202 and Hungary did little to dislodge the Venetians; a loyal Croatian noble won it back two years later, but within a year Venice held it again, this time by a treaty with the city council making them overseers instead of occupiers. Everyone knows the treaty is a sham: the wealth has only changed hands, which galls the locals more, and violence flares nightly on the docks and in the alleys, breeding Infernal auras (see the night streets). In history the risings go on for two centuries, until Venice gives the city back in 1358.

neighbours.name: Pula
neighbours.summary: An old Roman town of the Istrian coast, founded (its faeries say) by the Colchians who came after the Golden Fleece, over the faerie town of Diviægrad. It has the faeries' roofless arena and the Temple of Augustus, and King Solomon of Hungary lies buried there.

neighbours.name: The Bosnian Church (the Patarians)
neighbours.summary:
Bosnia's own church, formed from the Bogomils who lived through Stefan Nemanja's purge late in the last century, holding its own ground between the Roman and Greek Churches. Its people call themselves Patarians and keep the Bogomil teaching. A bishop, the djed, leads it with a council of twelve, the strojnici; it is a loose web of monastic houses (hiža), each under a gost with his own strojnici. It keeps out of politics and, beyond burials, has little to do with the Bosniaks.

Serbs and Croats put up with it as they put up with each other's rites, but Hungary does not, and a crusade is gathering against it.

details.rules: Bogomil doctrine; a loose network of monastic houses
details.wants: To be left alone between Rome and Constantinople
details.offers: Burials, and a school at Mostre

neighbours.name: The Redcap Families
neighbours.summary:
The Tribunal's sprawling Redcap clans, centred on Old Histria: messengers, touring players who carry letters and plays that sway the common folk, retired Redcaps keeping shops in most towns, and magi's spouses named Redcaps for the rights it gives them. Harco counts only fifteen proper Redcaps in Transylvania, the heads of families among them; the rest serve as the House's agents. Children of the local vampires, with their small useful powers, are sought out as recruits, and Harco will not accept those.

Whole families travel together, so when trouble strikes a whole troupe or a whole ship can vanish, and every oppidum is then formally asked for help.

details.rules: Heads of the main families meet yearly under the chief Mercere; members call each other cousin
details.wants: Recognition by Harco of all their kin as Redcaps
details.offers: Messages every week, travelling players, news, propaganda, guides in war

neighbours.name: Transylvania
neighbours.summary:
The land beyond the forest: a high plateau, on average some twelve hundred feet up, north and west of the Carpathians, which bend through the country like a reversed L. It is the eastern edge of the Kingdom of Hungary, governed for the king by a voivode, a prince appointed for a few years at a time, from Alba Iulia. South of the mountains more Vlach country runs down to the Danube, and east of them, past the Milcov and below the Cheremosh, hills fall away to plains and the Black Sea. The Romans called the whole of it Dacia.

Its peoples are many. The Vlachs, who call themselves rumân, are the oldest; the Hungarian kings have planted others as guards and settlers: Szeklers and Pechenegs at the passes, Saxons in seven walled towns, and lately the Teutonic Knights in the Burzenland, all set against the Cumans who roam beyond the eastern mountains. Hungarians, Slavs and Bulgarians live here too.

Hermetically it is the heart of House Tremere's Tribunal: Lycaneon, the Founder's first domus magna, lies in the mountains of Maramures in the north, Coeris nearby, and the Scholomance hides in a storm regio south of Hermannstadt. Dragons are common enough in the Carpathians to be only an uncommon sight.

Vis here (each in its place): the Furus brook at Ikafalva (Aquam, which the Scholomance gathers).

Horror seeds. This is the land of the book's horror stories. A vampire wearing the face of a dead friend or foe makes a fine nemesis; werewolves are common in places; vampire hunters serve as the savant who alone can beat the monster, or become monsters themselves, since a dhampir rises as a vampire when he dies, and a hunter whose own parent is the vampire has a ready-made tragedy. Giants make good brutes, with storm wizards, who hunt them, as the savant. The empty wilderness can drive the stoutest grog to frenzy, and a story locked into one regio, one storm or one night keeps the dread tight. Transylvania's dragons have been held in check since the second century by the Pax Draconis of Fetillusclaviceps, a Roman dragon who beat the twelve-headed Carpathian zmaj Abur-ciocîrlie in a duel and set the aždaja Slomljenakrila against the oath-breaking Britvazub; he has not been seen for fifty years, his lair is unknown, and some Tremere suspect the later sightings were magi in his likeness, as the Founder once was (see the Bestiary and the Dragon War).

links.note: the commonest vampire, wearing a dead villager's shape
the unseen vampire that haunts a dead man's kin
the formless sack the young vampire becomes

neighbours.name: Maramures
neighbours.summary:
The northern uplands of the Tribunal, high peaks round valleys cool in winter and oddly warm in summer. The terrain kept the Romans out, so the old Dacian rites lasted here longer than anywhere else in Hungary. Gold, silver, copper, lead, zinc and salt lie in its mountains, which is what drew Tremere to found Lycaneon here; Coeris lies in the same country.

The wolves of these mountains say their forebears were men who worshipped pagan gods in wolf shape.

neighbours.name: The Carpathian Mountains
neighbours.summary:
The great range that bends round Transylvania, crossed by a handful of passes the Hungarian kings guard with settled peoples. Dragons live here in such numbers that they are merely uncommon; the local dragon king, Aževastjepan, a seven-headed zmaj, holds his realm to the Pax Draconis without mercy and has banished the aždaje from it, with mixed success (see the Bestiary). No magus has met him and not even other dragons know his lair, though they speak of him with awe.

Some of the Tribunal's mountain lakes cast up flotsam and bones that suggest hidden passages to a sea, the Black, the Adriatic, or, some say, the Baltic.

Horror seed: the mountains' dragons, hundreds or thousands of them, can come as a single monster or as a horde (see the Dragon War).

neighbours.name: Kogaionon
neighbours.summary: A mountain the Geto-Dacians held holy, its exact place now uncertain. The Cult of Zalmoxis says its founder spent three years in a hidden cave near the summit before coming back to teach his people magic and the soul's immortality; others say he died there and rose again.

neighbours.name: The Sasar, River of the Ladies
neighbours.summary: The river below Lycaneon's mountain, from which the oppidum draws its water through tunnels underground. Its local name may recall the nymphs said to live deep in every stream that ends in the Danube, the handmaidens of the goddess Danu (the book gives no aura).

neighbours.name: Körösfö
neighbours.summary:
Fields where a rich mining town once stood. Its people grew so wealthy their children never learned to work or keep the Sabbath; they gave up the church for feasting, and at last chose it as the only hall big enough for a dance, without noticing the day was Good Friday. At the first step God sank the whole town into the earth. It carries an Infernal aura (the book gives no strength), and the damned are sometimes heard crying out under the fields.

Now and then a peasant turns up the great gold cross from the church spire, cannot scratch any gold off it, hides it while he fetches help and tools, and never finds it again. Perhaps God lets it surface so the virtuous can redeem the lost town; perhaps it is only a warning about unearned gold. Every ingot in Lycaneon's vault is stamped with the town's name, and visitors who ask are told why.

neighbours.name: The Burzenland
neighbours.summary:
The south-eastern corner of the Saxon country, inside the Carpathian ring, granted by Andrew II to the Teutonic Knights in 1211 to hold the passes against the Cumans. The Order judges its own people here and may found markets. In nine years it has raised several forts and is finishing five castles, Kronstadt in the middle and the other four about twenty miles apart round it, as bases for pushing into the Cuman lands, with Saxon settlers to feed them.

Under a holier Order (an optional take on the knights) the land they conquer carries a Dominion aura of Brave temper.

Horror seed: the Teutonic Knights can be the savants of a horror story, the hidden hand of a conspiracy, or, as a small band gone mad or bad, its psychopaths.

neighbours.name: Marienburg
neighbours.summary: A Teutonic castle in the Burzenland, one of the four outer castles, still being finished in 1220. With its fellows it anchors the Order's grip on the land and its advance on the Cumans (the book gives no aura).

neighbours.name: Kronstadt Castle
neighbours.summary: A Teutonic castle in the Burzenland, the central castle of the five, still being finished in 1220. With its fellows it anchors the Order's grip on the land and its advance on the Cumans (the book gives no aura).

neighbours.name: Rosenau
neighbours.summary: A Teutonic castle in the Burzenland, one of the four outer castles, still being finished in 1220. With its fellows it anchors the Order's grip on the land and its advance on the Cumans (the book gives no aura).

neighbours.name: Schwarzenburg
neighbours.summary: A Teutonic castle in the Burzenland, one of the four outer castles, still being finished in 1220. With its fellows it anchors the Order's grip on the land and its advance on the Cumans (the book gives no aura).

neighbours.name: Kreuzburg
neighbours.summary: A Teutonic castle in the Burzenland, one of the four outer castles, still being finished in 1220. With its fellows it anchors the Order's grip on the land and its advance on the Cumans (the book gives no aura).

neighbours.name: The Bran Pass
neighbours.summary:
The old, busy road through the southern Carpathians from Câmpulung to Kronstadt. Fortifying it has just begun: the leading voivode of Transylvania has a plain stone castle at its northern mouth, the Teutonic Knights two wooden ones along it, and the voivode of Câmpulung means to build at the southern end and hopes the Saxons will help. Whoever closes the pass could cut the southern plains off from Hungary and throw off his overlord, so any Tremere can see war coming; the House may be drawn in by any party, or may quietly wear all of them down to keep things as they are.

House Tremere has a zenodochium on a clifftop at the southern end (see the zenodochia). A band of southern knights has lately moved into it and preys on the traffic; their leader, a distant kinsman of the royal house, dreams of raising the Vlachs against the king. The elders want it back, a fitting test for young magi: kill them all and hide it, at the risk of royal notice, or find a quieter way.

neighbours.name: Ikafalva and the Furus
neighbours.summary:
A small Vlach village behind the Priest's Mountain, with the brook called the Furus running past it. Magyar legend says a mighty Magyar warrior, sworn to the goddess Furuzsina, won this land for his tribe and died in the last battle, and the spring rose where his blood fell; the neighbours believe the villagers are uncommonly strong from drinking it.

Vis: a pawn of Aquam can be drawn from the source under each full moon. It is easy to gather, and the Scholomance sends its older Gifted pupils to do it, except when the Vlachs and the Hungarian clans to the west, who both claim the brook, are fighting over it: then children may be caught in a skirmish and need rescuing.

neighbours.name: The Szekler Land
neighbours.summary:
The eastern edge of Hungary, where the kings have moved the Szekler tribes, a few at a time, to face the Cuman raiders; the Szeklers once lived further south, in what is now the Burzenland. Their count usually rules from near Miercurea Ciuc. Giants live here under a king of their own, and the faeries under two queens: the good Firtos and the evil Tartos (see the Bestiary).

Should the Szeklers ever face destruction, the ghosts of Attila's army rise from the grave to defend them.

links.note: two giant brothers forever quarrelling over a fence

neighbours.name: The Palace of Balbona
neighbours.summary: Each new giant king of the Szekler land builds himself a new palace and leaves his predecessor's empty, so several old giant palaces stand in the region. The best known was Balbona's, who called his giants to council with huge golden bells. They were buried deep when he died, yet on feast days they still ring underground and shake the earth, harmlessly.

neighbours.name: The Golden Palace of Firtos
neighbours.summary: The palace of gold of Firtos, queen of the good faeries of the Szekler land (the book gives no aura).

neighbours.name: The Palace of Tartos
neighbours.summary: The hall of Tartos, queen of the evil faeries of the Szekler land, lit by three diamonds as big as a man's head hanging on golden chains. Her hoard holds gold bars, golden lions with carbuncle eyes, a golden hen with her chicks, and golden casks of coin (the book gives no aura).

neighbours.name: Cumania
neighbours.summary: The steppe and hills beyond the eastern Carpathians, where the Cuman tribes graze their herds; once the Pechenegs' west. There are no towns, which makes the land easy to seize and hard to keep: an expelled tribe, helped by its neighbours, wears any invader down and returns. In summer the Cumans draw back to their camps south of the mountains to tend their stock.

neighbours.name: The Mountain of Lycaneon
neighbours.summary:
A forested peak among high, steep mountains above a valley in Maramures, hollowed out by Terram magic into sixteen square levels, each a little wider than the one above, linked by five shafts (one in the middle, and one from each corner of the ninth level) that are crossed by flying devices, the plainest being wooden pallets the covenfolk ride with their loads; stairs and trapdoors are rarely used. The endless-seeming maze of passages is a deliberate confusion for outsiders. Tunnels run down to the Sasar for water.

On the summit, wreathed in storm cloud, stand six strong basalt buildings joined in a hexagon, Romanesque work of Tremere's own design, with a curved tower at each corner, so that the whole looks like an enormous black crown; a broad dark road lined with golden imperial statues leads to its great doors.

Its Magic aura reaches 9 in places, but those parts warp, and with room to spare they are mostly left empty. The white wolves of the mountain, its old guardians, give the place its name (see the Bestiary).

neighbours.name: The Valley of the Scholomance
neighbours.summary:
A lonely valley high in the Carpathians south of Hermannstadt, holding only a small lake with no name, glassy on still days and mirroring the whole sky, and a Magic aura of 3. Travellers' tales tell of a castle over a high pass that shows only in the heart of a storm and is gone when the storm-tossed seek shelter there; locals nod and call it the Scholomance.

Storm wizards (see the hedge traditions) have twice banded together to storm the tower, using their powers to stop it slipping back into its regio, and were beaten off both times; they spoke only of taking back something they had lost. The dragon king of the Carpathians around the Scholomance is Aževastjepan, a seven-headed zmaj who keeps the Pax Draconis harshly and bars aždaje from his realm; no magus has met him and even other dragons don't know his lair, and a few magi have noticed how like the Scholomance's caretaker's his name sounds.

levels.name: The Scholomance
levels.see: Only in a violent storm, when lightning plays about the crags
levels.enter: Open to anyone while the storm lasts; it vanishes as readily as it appears
levels.notes: The tower stands on a cliff above a little-used pass. Now and then it appears elsewhere, mostly in the Tribunal's mountains but once in a desert sandstorm; the headmaster can steer its showings in the valley, but not its rare far wanderings.

neighbours.secrets: There may be a second, deeper level of the regio known only to the headmaster; this has never been confirmed or denied. Whether the storm wizards want the tower or something hidden in it is unknown.

neighbours.name: The Voivode of Transylvania
neighbours.summary: The king's governor of Transylvania, a prince in all but name, appointed from a line of voivodes who each hold the post only a few years; the book does not name the present one. He rules from Alba Iulia as the King of Hungary's vassal. The leading voivode has built a stone castle at the northern mouth of the Bran Pass, and a firm border there could tempt him toward independence. He might ask magi to help destroy a Teutonic castle.

neighbours.name: The Voivode of Câmpulung
neighbours.summary: The strongest Vlach lord south of the Carpathians, vassal of a greater neighbour, ruling from Câmpulung. He plans a fortress at the southern end of the Bran Pass and hopes his Saxon neighbours will help build it; he might ask magi too. Closing the pass would loosen the southern plains from Hungary.

neighbours.name: The Burzenland
neighbours.summary:
The Teutonic Knights' land in Transylvania, granted by Andrew II in 1211, just after he agreed a match between his daughter and the son of Hermann of Thuringia. The king gave the territory and freedom from taxes and dues, but kept the right to mint coin and half of all gold and silver mined; in return the knights guard the Carpathian passes against the Cumans. The Order may hold its own courts and found markets here.

Brother Theoderich, master of the mission, runs it almost alone, since the hochmeister divides his time between the Holy Land and Egypt. Fast expansion, Theoderich's want of tact and the envy of the Hungarian lords make an explosive mix; the knights have already offended the local bishop by denying his rights in the Burzenland, and they court the pope to slip free of the Hungarian crown.

neighbours.name: Alba Iulia
neighbours.summary: The White Castle, capital of Transylvania and seat of its voivode, the King of Hungary's vassal. It stands on the foundations of Apulum, one of the largest cities of Roman Dacia.

neighbours.name: Câmpulung
neighbours.summary: The chief town south of the mountains, on the remains of a Roman colony, fifteen miles below the Bran Pass; seat of the voivode of Câmpulung.

neighbours.name: The Villages of Lycaneon
neighbours.summary: The small towns round Lycaneon, peopled by descendants of the miners Tremere brought, retired grogs and the heirs of the oppidum's craftsmen. They speak a Latin dialect, mostly read and write, and reckon like merchants; each elects three leaders to a council they call a Tribunal, which settles borders, trade and crime, and women often lead. Their warriors are mountain skirmishers with bows, axes and short swords, and their odd wares go round the Tribunal with the Redcaps.

neighbours.name: Bistritz
neighbours.summary: Bistritz, one of the seven fortified towns of the Transylvanian Saxons that give Siebenbürgen its name: German settlers living by their own laws as royal guests, who farm, raise stock and work mines.

neighbours.name: Hermannstadt
neighbours.summary: Hermannstadt, one of the seven fortified towns of the Transylvanian Saxons that give Siebenbürgen its name: German settlers living by their own laws as royal guests, who farm, raise stock and work mines. The Scholomance's valley lies in the mountains to the south.

neighbours.name: Klausenburg
neighbours.summary: Klausenburg, one of the seven fortified towns of the Transylvanian Saxons that give Siebenbürgen its name: German settlers living by their own laws as royal guests, who farm, raise stock and work mines.

neighbours.name: Kronstadt
neighbours.summary: Kronstadt, one of the seven fortified towns of the Transylvanian Saxons that give Siebenbürgen its name: German settlers living by their own laws as royal guests, who farm, raise stock and work mines. It lies in the Burzenland, round the central castle of the Teutonic Knights, and at the northern end of the Bran Pass.

neighbours.name: Mediasch
neighbours.summary: Mediasch, one of the seven fortified towns of the Transylvanian Saxons that give Siebenbürgen its name: German settlers living by their own laws as royal guests, who farm, raise stock and work mines.

neighbours.name: Mühlbach
neighbours.summary: Mühlbach, one of the seven fortified towns of the Transylvanian Saxons that give Siebenbürgen its name: German settlers living by their own laws as royal guests, who farm, raise stock and work mines.

neighbours.name: Schässburg
neighbours.summary: Schässburg, one of the seven fortified towns of the Transylvanian Saxons that give Siebenbürgen its name: German settlers living by their own laws as royal guests, who farm, raise stock and work mines.

neighbours.name: The Teutonic Knights
neighbours.summary:
Formally the Hospital Order of St Mary of the Germans in Jerusalem, youngest of the military orders: founded at the siege of Acre after Barbarossa's death, when crusaders from Bremen and Lübeck set up a hospital for sick Germans the Hospitallers neglected, approved by Celestine III and given a military charter in 1198. Its head, the hochmeister, is elected for life by the general chapter; Hermann von Salza has held the post since 1210, travelling as diplomat and inspector with a council of the masters, the treasurer, the grand commander and the marshal. In 1220 it has its seat at Acre and just two missions, in the Empire and in Transylvania, where Brother Theoderich is master.

Its rule, the customs, is written in German: poverty, chastity and obedience, the canonical hours, priestly dress under a white mantle with a black cross, no rowdy feasts and no women. Punishment runs from the whip and short rations to years in chains; cowardice before the enemy, desertion to the infidel and sodomy mean expulsion or death. Each knight has ten graymantles, half-brothers of common birth, as squires and sergeants. Knights are noble, some from the Empire's serf-knights and poor; many carry relics, often in their sword hilts, and study Theology, Church Lore and Dominion Lore beside arms (Brother Chaplain, Brother Knight and Brother Sergeant are their Virtues: black cross on green, white and grey).

The Order and House Tremere want much the same, a self-ruling state for mankind's good under their own guidance. The knights mean to push down the Danube from the Burzenland to the Black Sea with garrisoned forts and reopen the land road to Constantinople. The pope has charged them to hunt heresy and diabolism, so the Tremere fear they would call the Order of Hermes heretic or pagan, and the House forbids Tribunal magi any formal contact; the knights will not stay ignorant long. The hochmeister seeks the Scholomance but has found only the same tale told again and thinks it a legend; a papal legate, sent by Honorius III to look into it, lodges with the knights.

Story: a hedge wizard with a grudge against the Order is taken by a Teutonic garrison and tells them all he knows of magi. When the garrison starts marking Hermetic targets, the troupe must decide how much to reveal, which the Tremere ban on contact forbids, or whether to wipe out the garrison and leave no witness.

details.wants: The Burzenland free of Hungary under the pope, and a road of forts down the Danube to the Black Sea
details.offers: Knights and garrisons against the Cumans; a hand of friendship, not always sincere

neighbours.secrets:
Two optional Orders. A holier one fights for the Dominion: its conquests carry a Brave Dominion aura, it sends preachers among the Cumans before its armies, and an inner circle of Divine wonder-workers uses Invocation, Blessing and Cursing and senses holiness. Their Blessing of the relic (Invocation 30) lends one relic's Magic Resistance and its scourge of demons to up to ten men who keep together, for a Sabbath.

A profane one serves infernal masters, wants power over land more than pagan blood, and hoards occult lore, capturing shamans, witches and taltós; many of its leaders are goetic sorcerers and the rest diabolists, and it rules the common folk through fear, possession and blackmail. Its favoured knights carry great swords with a bound demon that whispers in their dreams, and that can trade a blow's damage for an Incapacitating wound that heals the wielder's own worst wound, three times a day (Consumption 37).

If history runs its course, Andrew II (home from crusade since 1218) is forced to grant the Golden Bull in 1222 but will not take the Burzenland back; in 1225 Hermann von Salza puts it under the Holy See, and the king drives the knights out by force when they refuse to go. The Cumans then pour through the weakened defences.

neighbours.name: The Transylvanian Saxons
neighbours.summary:
German settlers, mostly from Saxony, who began coming in the middle of the last century and came in numbers under the Teutonic Knights, who need their grain, wool and meat to stand on their own. They mine gold and silver for the knights (half goes to the crown) and iron, which they trade or smelt. Like the Szeklers they are free royal guests (hospites in Hungarian law, not the Hermetic privilege), outside the counts' reach, and a tax on them yields a share of the king's income.

Their land, wider than the knights' own, they call Siebenbürgen after its seven chief walled towns: Hermannstadt, Kronstadt, Bistritz, Klausenburg, Schässburg, Mediasch and Mühlbach; the Burzenland is only its south-eastern corner.

details.wants: Land, markets and their own law
details.offers: Grain, wool, meat, metal and miners; help building castles

neighbours.name: The Szeklers
neighbours.summary:
Frontier guards, as their name says, and by their own account the remnant of Attila's Huns, left by his son to hold a foothold for the Huns' return; they allied with the Magyars, who claimed the same descent, and now speak Hungarian but remain a class apart. Six tribes of four branches each, every branch owing a hundred horsemen in war; pasture and plough land belong to the branch, and who uses which field each year is settled by shooting arrows. Branch war leaders and officers form the upper class over farmers and herdsmen, and to Hungarian eyes they all answer to a count near Miercurea Ciuc, though it is less simple than that.

They lead the king's army out and guard its rear coming home, more of them if he leads in person, but do not fight to the north or west, sending hired men instead. In return all are free and untaxed, though each household gives the king a branded ox when he is crowned, weds or has an heir. Their light horse archers suit Cuman raiders better than Byzantines. They are reputed the fiercest fighters in the Tribunal, with a tradition of taltós who led them in war (see the hedge traditions). Lately a mysterious preacher has stirred them to turn on their neighbours, and Vlachs say a taltós has won back his tradition's power and is gathering lesser taltós into an empire.

details.wants: Their freedom and common lands kept
details.offers: Horse archers, light cavalry and infantry for the king

neighbours.name: The Pechenegs
neighbours.summary: Once a loose league of nomad warriors ruling the west of what is now Cumania. Beaten by the Byzantines and robbed of their lands, they became Christian and the Hungarian kings settled them in the southern Carpathians, where they now guard the passes once held against them, as royal guests in Hungarian law. They speak Oghuz. Many of their warriors took service with magi when they lost their lands, and their shamans entered House Tremere's service then too (see the hedge traditions).

details.offers: Warriors for the king and for the oppida

neighbours.name: The Cumans
neighbours.summary:
The Kipchaks: nomads who took the lands east of the Carpathians in the eleventh century, a confederation stretching deep into Asia with no single leader, its tribes raiding, settling, trading and treating with outsiders on their own account. Most are Turkic or Alan; most still roam, though some farm. They speak Kipchak. Fear of them made the kings move Szekler tribes to the passes and bring in the Teutonic Knights, and the kings use the threat of them, or of a Cuman marriage, to wring favours from the pope.

They are kin to Bulgaria's Asen rulers, sheltered and armed the rebellion against Byzantium, and still serve Bulgaria as mercenaries; their summer withdrawal to tend their herds shapes Bulgarian campaigning. In battle they strike lightly armoured, feign flight again and again, then turn with a roar and swords drawn. Their religion is Tengrist, worship of a creator sky god; their shamans scry, rule the weather, heal fast and travel swiftly (see the hedge traditions). None seem as strong as Bulgaria's old shamans; some Tremere think something besides the Church destroyed those, others that strong Cuman shamans simply stay out of border wars.

If history runs on, the Mongols break them at the Kalka in 1223; twenty thousand families settle in Hungary as Christians sworn to fight the Mongols, others vanish into the Golden Horde, and more flee to Nicaea's service.

neighbours.name: The Vlachs
neighbours.summary:
The native people north of the Danube, rumân or roman in their own tongue, heirs of the Getae and the Dacians Romanised under Rome and left behind as farmers and shepherds when Rome withdrew in 275. Visigoths, Huns, Gepids and Avars drove them into the wilds; Slavs, Magyars and Pechenegs came and settled beside them, each leaving only a mark. They bend to foreign rule and endure.

Their nobles, the boyars, take the titles jupan, cneaz or voievod, each equal to a duke, and live with war bands among villages of bound peasants. Free peasants form obote, self-governing communes with elected officers and common land, paying tribute to the Hungarian crown and free to move away; communes outnumber boyar villages, more so in the east. They were Christian early, by legend through the Apostle Andrew in the Dobrogea, and their bishops look to Rome, not Constantinople.

Their folk witches, the vrajitoarele, belong to the Magic realm, not the Infernal (see the hedge traditions).

details.wants: Their land and their ways, under whatever ruler
details.offers: Shepherds, farmers, local knowledge and boyar war bands

neighbours.name: The Brodnici
neighbours.summary: A people of mixed Vlach and Slav stock, the main group in the lands east of the Carpathians, which have no city of their own and are far more independent than the western Vlach lands. They owe allegiance to Suzdal; the other groups there serve stronger Vlach and Transylvanian voivodes, and the region is not united.

neighbours.name: The Cult of Zalmoxis
neighbours.summary:
The secret faith of the old Geto-Dacian elite, who worshipped the one god Zalmoxis before Christ; driven underground and into the mountains as others converted, it survives among rich, proud, stubborn families as a mystery cult whose rites only a few see. Its tale makes Zalmoxis a pupil of Pythagoras on Samos who learned of immortality and rebirth in Egypt, then spent three years in a cave on Kogaionon and came back to teach (or died and rose again). Herodotus and Plato call him a man and Christian writers a fraud, but that they all tell the story at all is unsettling. Every five years the cult sends him a messenger by throwing a man onto a spear point: if he dies the god has accepted him.

Princes and priests suspect it lives on in several Vlach lands. In the mountains south of Maramures several groups follow vrajitoarele, Vlach folk witches of the Magic realm. One Gifted leader is slowly drawing the others to him, against the distrust his Gift stirs, and on learning that a wizard of the hollow mountain nearby is called Zalmoxis he proclaims the god risen again and imprisoned by the other wizards. Lycaneon's magi know nothing of it.

neighbours.name: Coeris
neighbours.summary: A mountain above a river in a valley of Maramures, carved by magic into a stair of terraces, its inside hollowed into rooms made for every purpose. The buildings outside are severe and geometric yet oddly graceful, the work of many hands over centuries with nothing that looks added on; centuries of limewash make the walls shine white, and many roofs are slates of rhodochrosite, banded red, white and pink. Every tree within a mile has been cleared, though oak and birch forest still surrounds it. The book gives no aura.

neighbours.name: The Altar of the Standards and the Gate of Eurydice
neighbours.summary:
A cave deep under Coeris. In it is a cleft in the earth said to be the road Orpheus took to the underworld, which the Tremere call the Gate of Eurydice. Niches line the cave, one for every Tremere who has died, most holding their sigils, the Founder's among them.

Asked about it, the Tremere say only that the magi who were here before the Founder took it for Orpheus's path to Hades, that they keep no Orphic rites and have no proof, and that there are many such caves.

levels.name: The City Below
levels.enter: Through the Gate of Eurydice, which is always open.
levels.notes: An insula of the Magic Realm, House Tremere's last refuge; the book gives no aura.

neighbours.secrets:
The Gate is a permanent, open way into the Magic Realm, to an insula the Tremere call the City Below: the place Coeris's people will withdraw to if the oppidum can no longer be held, almost an afterlife, though perhaps one the House could come back from once its enemies stop watching. The book gives no aura for it.

A troupe may prefer another answer: a Portal to a warded cemetery far off in Africa or Asia; a fortress deep in Faerie built as a last refuge in the Sundering; a prison for Diedne magi, still alive since no one ages in the Magic Realm; or a pleasant garden where a cheerful old man named Tremere grows roses among the ghosts of his family, plays with his wolf and wonders whether his brother will call.

neighbours.name: Dragonesti
neighbours.summary: A large town a mile and a half east of Coeris. Its people are free, but own that the town stands on the wizards' land; magic made its stone walls, paved streets, sewers and wells. It feeds Coeris and sends it craftsmen, and its taxes are lighter than anywhere else in Hungary. Its folk are Christian but wary of strangers, priests included.
neighbours.ruler: Free townsfolk on the land of Coeris

neighbours.name: The church of Dragonesti
neighbours.summary: One of two splendid churches, at Coeris and in Dragonesti, raised by ritual magic to learn whether consecration would bring them down; had it, House Tremere could have turned consecration into a weapon against the Order's beloved towers. They stood, and the experiment failed. The Bishop of Transylvania appoints their priests.

neighbours.name: The church of Coeris
neighbours.summary: One of two splendid churches, at Coeris and in Dragonesti, raised by ritual magic to learn whether consecration would bring them down; had it, House Tremere could have turned consecration into a weapon against the Order's beloved towers. They stood, and the experiment failed. The Bishop of Transylvania appoints their priests.

neighbours.name: Sarmizegethusa Fort
neighbours.summary:
The first fort Norsius built, raised in the ruins of Sarmizegethusa, the palace of the Dacian king Decebalus in the second century, near the heart of the Tribunal. It is Kezdö Válasz's one fixed home and the only fort never abandoned at the seven-year move: it keeps a standing staff, two laboratories traditionally the leader's and his partner's (often empty, since both have other labs where their sanctum markers hang), and the oppidum's casting tablets, vis stores and spare gear. The magi gather here every 12 August.

Like every Kezdö fort it is a two-storey stone block with one door, slit windows and a taller watchtower at one corner: a kitchen and great hall below, and stairs in the thickness of the walls, one up to the upper floor and the tower, one down to the cellars. Forts are always set in a Magic aura; the book gives no strength (5 is the pack's).

neighbours.name: The Prokletije Fort
neighbours.summary: Leona's new fort in the Prokletije, the 'Accursed Mountains' of southern Serbia at the far end of the Dinaric Alps, near the source of the Erenick River, where Macrobius was killed by a griffin. Remote and hard to reach, it is her base for hunting griffins; her sodales grumble that it wastes the oppidum's casting tablets and vis, and Essedarius promises it will be given up once her anger cools. Neculai has been sent to call on her. Magic aura, strength not given (4 is the pack's).

neighbours.name: The Abandoned Forts of Kezdö Válasz
neighbours.summary:
Forts Kezdö Válasz has left behind in the seven-yearly moves, scattered across the Tribunal in places that no longer interest it. A fort that drew mundane notice is cleared away, and one that drew supernatural notice is destroyed, by casting tablets made for the purpose; others are left standing for later use, or simply because the tablet to destroy them was not to hand. Abandoned forts are usually left empty. All were built in Magic auras, but auras change: some are still Magic, a few are now Faerie, and one or two Infernal. The book dates none of them.

Story seeds: wandering coloniae who know the oppidum's ways may squat in one, and if a powerful one settles in a fort the oppidum wants back, the youngest members are sent to deal with it; giants looking for a home near a village, a magical dragon in a mountain fort, or knights or bandits looking for a refuge may move in too.
neighbours.secrets: Whether a fort left standing still belongs to Kezdö Válasz once its magi have gone is an open question.

neighbours.name: The Iron Gate
neighbours.summary:
The gorge where the Danube cuts between the Carpathian and Balkan mountains, dividing its upper and lower valleys; one of the places Kezdö Válasz might build a fort. Remnants of the Bridge of Apollodorus, built under Trajan and broken a century later, still stand, and ghostly legionaries are said to march across it under the full moon.

Story seed: fearing war between Hungary and the Bošnjanin, Essedarius gives young magi vis and casting tablets to raise a fort here, and wonders whether a regio still holds a magical copy of the bridge, which would account for the ghosts.

neighbours.name: The Vargyas River
neighbours.summary:
A small river running off the western slopes of the Hargitta mountains, which might be the lost Sargetias. When Trajan marched on Dacia in 105, Decebalus had captive Romans turn the Sargetias aside, sealed his and his nobles' gold and silver into its bed under stones, let the water back, hid more in caves along its banks, and killed the workmen. Captured Dacian nobles betrayed the secret, but a Byzantine official's report says the hoard was never recovered and says nothing of the caves. Neither river nor caves has been found.

Kezdö Válasz has not looked for it: the hoard is small beside Lycaneon's.
neighbours.secrets: Slavonic dragons line their lairs with gold and silver, and a treasure this size has very probably drawn one.

neighbours.name: The Bran Pass Zenodochium
neighbours.summary:
A zenodochium House Tremere built in the Bran Pass, an important road, atop a sheer cliff at the pass's southern end. A band of southern knights has lately moved in and preys on the merchants passing below; their leader, kin at some remove to the royal house, is a rebel who hopes to raise the Vlachs against the royal army.

Story seed: the House's elders want it back and send young magi; killing the knights and hiding the bodies may bring the king's men, and a subtler way may be wiser.

neighbours.name: The Plague House
neighbours.summary:
A rural zenodochium near a village whose people have found it and learnt that the sick who lie in its hall usually get better. They use it as a pest house: at the first sign of illness the strong men carry the sick there and come back a month later to collect them or bury them.

Story seed: grogs bring their badly hurt magus in and find Lucia, a village girl, near death of plague in the hall; the grogs may take her for an intruder, a servant or a maga, and the villagers, returning, may think the Gifted stranger means harm to their refuge, all the more if Lucia has died. The Tribunal does not mind villagers using it, so long as they keep it in repair.

neighbours.name: The Lost Zenodochium of Zadar
neighbours.summary: After the bloodshed of 1203 the Tremere set up a zenodochium inside a regio, in a magical lacuna in Zadar, and, expecting more bloodshed, staffed it with a skilled surgeon and some helpers. Within months the House lost touch with them, and the regio itself seems to have vanished. The search has dwindled, but young magi still try now and then to find the surgeon. The book gives no aura.
neighbours.secrets: Zadar's violence breeds Infernal auras and regiones over its worst killings; what became of the lacuna and its people is left to the storyguide.

neighbours.name: Leviathan's Cache
neighbours.summary: A hidden naval base somewhere among the southern Dalmatian islands, its place undisclosed, where House Tremere keeps the stores to support its small Adriatic fleet in a war. The book gives no aura.

neighbours.name: Gigas
neighbours.summary:
A covenant of the Theban Tribunal, a hunting lodge south-west of Sofia, well to the north-west of Evredika's sancta in the Rhodopes. It is House Tremere's thinly veiled cat's paw among the Theban magi (described in The Sundered Eagle and the Theban pack), and has been told not to contest the vis Evredika claims. Not a Transylvanian oppidum, so not a covenant here. The Theban book gives it a weak Magic aura (1 here).

Story seed: a hunting party led by a nobleman with a 'pet' white wolf strips all of Evredika's vis sources, and Gigas is the obvious suspect. If its denials are true, who is framing it, and why?
neighbours.secrets: The book leaves the true raiders to the storyguide.

neighbours.name: The Storm Wizards
neighbours.summary:
A lonely, ancient Gifted tradition found only in Transylvania. Mountain villagers have long exposed unwanted babies (the deformed, the seemingly mad, the children of incest) on the bare slopes to rid themselves of whatever curse they feared; nearly all die, but the few with The Gift are carried off by bearded giants striding above the storm clouds, and so the storm wizards find their apprentices and open their Gift. The grown wizards are huge, bearded and solitary.

Magi know only that they raise and steer storms and are said to number fewer than six; peasants blame every storm on them, and since a called storm looks wholly natural, nobody can be sure there are not many more. Being Gifted, they fall under Join or Die, but they are so rare and seem so harmless that hardly any magus has found out. Some joined House Ex Miscellanea in the Schism War and fought beside the Tremere, a service the Order has forgotten; no text on their powers is known to survive. Their aims, if they have any, are unknown.

Twice they have banded together to storm the Scholomance's tower, holding it out of its regio, and twice been driven off; they talk of taking back something they lost. A Transylvanian tale of a dragon-riding weather wizard, the tenth scholar the Devil keeps from the Scholomance, may owe something to them. Thietmar is one of them.

Story seeds: travellers caught in a mountain storm see, by the lightning, a giant fleeing bolts that keep finding him, and must choose whether to help the giant or the young wizard whose initiation they have walked into; or they find an ice cave carved with runes and full of Auram vis, and with it the wizards who harvest it.

A member is played from the tradition record the faction names: its powers are summarised here, and what the record only notes is in Against the Dark (chapter nine) and Hedge Magic Revised Edition.

Their magic: three Supernatural Abilities, Storm Calling (Communication + ability: raise a storm, local, provincial or national, lasting from a Diameter to a Moon, for 1, 2 or 4 pawns of Auram vis, or move any storm without cost, even against the wind or indoors), Storm Riding (Perception + ability: see from, travel to, or send a touched person to any point of a storm in sight) and Storm Fighting (buffets, deluge, hail, erosion that topples a building, and lightning at +20), with the Arcane Ability Organization Lore: Storm Wizards and Penetration. Once raised a storm is natural, so it needs no Penetration and crosses an Aegis. In a season of ice harvesting a wizard gathers (Int + Organization Lore + aura) / 3 pawns of Auram vis as ice that never melts, at sites he keeps secret. A wizard who takes two or more Warping Points at once, or reaches a new Warping Score, may become a storm for a Moon (Strength + stress die against 3 + Warping Score), and dies if he cannot gather himself again before it blows out. The Heart of the Storm initiation (Ease Factor 21, script bonus +15: the giant's heart as a Quest, the Feud with the giants' tribe as a Major Ordeal) gives Giant Blood, free to a storm wizard. The Virtues Storm Calling, Storm Riding and Storm Fighting and the Social Status Storm Wizard are in the catalog.

details.rules: Every one is Gifted, nearly every one a man; each lives alone in a cave high above the snow. An apprentice ends his training by hunting down a true giant and eating its heart.
details.wants: Their ice sites kept secret; giants hunted; to be let alone
details.offers: Storms moved away from a village, for gifts of food left out

neighbours.secrets: The Tremere may be burying what they know of the storm wizards on purpose: their powers baffled the Diedne in the Schism War, and the House may want that surprise kept for the next war.

neighbours.name: A storm wizards' ice cave
neighbours.summary:
A cave high in the Carpathians whose frozen walls are cut with strange runes and pictures of shadowy giants walking over stormy peaks: one of the sites where the storm wizards harvest their ice, which they guard as their deepest secret. Its Magic aura is strong (the book gives no number); where it lies is left to the storyguide.

Vis: Auram, soaked into the ice of the walls, drawn out with a spell like Gather the Essence of the Beast (amount not given). Magi who use it will have to share or fight for it with the storm wizards, who are angry at first but may be talked round to trade or alliance.

neighbours.name: The Fectores
neighbours.summary:
House Tremere's corps of monster hunters, named from interfectores, slayers. A century ago the vampire of a dead dhampir magus was trying to fill the House with vampires; the famed hunter Murat of Terezin came to Coeris and with Radomir of Tremere cleared every one out. Murat joined House Ex Miscellanea, and the two used a hoard of initiation scripts, a Gnostic's notes on a taltós clan he had spied on, to learn how to open a Gifted person to the Hunters' Arts. Laniena, by the Aggtelek caves, trains them (see the Hungary chapter).

Two in three of the Gifted children Laniena finds are trained as Fectores: peasants, soldiers and dhampirs with no taste for fifteen years of books, three of them made in the time one apprentice takes. The other third become Hermetic Fectores, magi Ex Miscellanea who also hold one Practice Art. Those who prove untrustworthy never swear the Oath and are spent where the danger is worst. Some magi call the training a deprivation of magical power, since the trainees could have learnt the Hermetic Arts; Laniena answers that they are not yet members of the Order, and the Tribunal, which is to say House Tremere, lets it go on. Bendis is the best of the non-Hermetic Fectores.

A member is played from the tradition record the faction names: its powers are summarised here, and what the record only notes is in Against the Dark (chapter nine) and Hedge Magic Revised Edition.

The Hunters' Arts, the scattered remnant of the old taltós magic: three Practice Arts like Techniques, Scry, Ban and Slay (each a Major Supernatural Virtue), joined with Foe Arts like narrow Forms (Minor Virtues; the first Practice Art brings one free). All are Difficult Arts, raised on the Ability table; against a mortal foe with no Might every level is 10 higher. Scry forges a lasting bond to a foe (Per + Scry + Foe + aura) that gives its direction, then its smells, sounds or sight, and a sympathetic bonus; a botch ties the foe to the scryer. Ban makes amulets lasting a Sun from twelve hours' work, one soaking up wounds from the foe and one cutting short its powers, and staked hawthorn wards that lower the Might of a foe inside for three days. Slay charges a new weapon in a day's chanting; each true fact about the foe lowers the level by 5 and each false one raises it, and a hit that penetrates leaves the foe Incapacitated, after which the weapon is spent. A Fector has The Gift, the free Fector Social Status, Second Sight, all three Practice Arts and three Foe Arts, 120 experience points from training, and no magical defence but Ban; the Fectores know the Foes Vampire, Werewolf, Ghost, Nightwalker and Witch. Hermetic Fectores take a Practice Art as their Major non-Hermetic Virtue, a Minor Magical Focus against their foe, and Weak Spontaneous Magic. The Virtues Fector, Scry Art, Ban Art, Slay Art and the Foe Art are in the catalog.
neighbours.ruler: The magi of Laniena, for House Tremere

details.rules: Gifted hunters trained at Laniena for five years in the Hunters' Arts; most then join House Ex Miscellanea as Gifted companions and learn the Parma Magica, but owe their loyalty to House Tremere. No dhampir may be given Hermetic training.
details.wants: Vampires and other supernatural threats destroyed
details.offers: Trained hunters, Hermetic or not, on the Tribunal's front line

links.note: Teaches them the Ban Art; Hermetic Fector

neighbours.secrets: Murat of Terezin was a dhampir and rose as a vampire when he died: he is now a kukudhi living far from Laniena with his fourth mortal wife and has fathered over twenty dhampir children. Only Murat the Younger knows, and lets him be for the hunters his children make.

neighbours.name: The Sabotnici
neighbours.summary:
Those born on a Saturday, a day many vampires cannot go out on or harm anyone born on: such a vampire's direct powers do not touch them. The Bulgarians call them sabotnici, the rest of the Balkans vaperari, the Greeks alaphroiskiotoi. A child born in the Unclean Days between Christmas and Epiphany, or in the Wolf Holiday of November, is a sabotnik too, but will rise as a vampire after death; the Wolf Holiday's children often turn into wolves and become pricolici when they die.

Not every sabotnik hunts. Many sense the unseen, and can find a vampire even when it has no body, or tell a magician or witch. Most who gain powers are men; the few women are stronger, and read dreams. Dogs can be sabotnici too, the four-eyed dogs with a black mark over each eye: Zuban is one (see the Bestiary). Looking through the sleeve of a sabotnik's shirt shows whether a corpse is a vampire, though the vampire may strike whoever is looking.

A member is played from the tradition record the faction names: its powers are summarised here, and what the record only notes is in Against the Dark (chapter nine) and Hedge Magic Revised Edition.

A sabotnik should take Second Sight, perhaps Magic Sensitivity, and a woman Dream Interpretation; one who hunts most likely knows the Scry Art. In a team of hunters they research the foe, gather its connections and track it.

details.rules: None: a sabotnik is made by the day of his birth, not by any school
details.offers: Finding vampires, and safety from their direct powers

neighbours.name: The Glogove
neighbours.summary:
Hunters marked at birth across the Balkans: born feet first, with teeth, or with red hair. They take their name from glog, the black hawthorn, a strong defence against vampires, and carve staves and swords from it, mostly to guard rather than to strike. Where a sabotnik finds vampires, a glog shields people from them and sometimes kills them. Glogove are hot-tempered and quarrelsome, often in trouble with their neighbours, and usually strong and athletic.

Black hawthorn grows slowly and twists, too crooked for planks; as a material it gives +7 to protect from vampires, +4 to protect from evil and +4 to prevent disease. Laniena has grown a hedge of it around its houses.

A member is played from the tradition record the faction names: its powers are summarised here, and what the record only notes is in Against the Dark (chapter nine) and Hedge Magic Revised Edition.

A glog should take Second Sight and often Warrior, an Affinity or Puissant Single Weapon, and too often Wrathful or Fury; a trained one knows the Ban or Slay Art. In a team they fight the foe hand to hand and ward the ground and their allies.

details.rules: None: a glog is marked at birth (feet first, with teeth, or red-haired)
details.offers: Protection from vampires, and their destruction

neighbours.name: The Taltós
neighbours.summary:
Hungarian magicians born to fight evil. A taltós who wins the childhood dream-fight becomes a nightwalker, one of a band whose spirits go out while they sleep to fight evil things and keep their villages safe. Among the Székely they were shape-changing shamans who led their warriors to war.

More than a thousand years ago the taltós were a mighty tradition of the Balkans, the wise men of the Huns, with powers from shapeshifting and spirit-walking to potions and vampire slaying. Quarrelsome, and made worse by The Gift, they split into factions as their tribes went to war; one side turned its vampire-killing magic on rival taltós, the other copied it, and within a few years they had all but wiped each other out. Today's taltós keep only scraps, and the Hunters' Arts descend from the same wreck.
